reading.rtitle: Why the Minutes Are Written Like That
paras: Anybody who has read the minutes of a meeting they attended has noticed that the document is stranger than the room. In the room, somebody said the file was sent to the wrong address. In the minutes, the file was sent to the wrong address. The person disappears. This is often described as corporate cowardice, and sometimes it is, but the habit exists for a reason that is worth understanding before you decide to break it.

A record is read by people who were not there, and it is read later, when the situation has moved. If a name is written next to a mistake, the name is what gets remembered, and everything after it is read as a defence. The passive removes the person from the sentence and leaves the fact, which is what the record is for. This is also why the same document will say, two lines further down, that the correction was approved by the finance director. When the news is good, or when accountability matters, the name comes back.

The skill, then, is not to write everything in the passive. It is to know which half of the meeting each sentence belongs to. Facts that could embarrass somebody: passive, and no name. Decisions and owners: active, with the name, because an action item without a name is not an action item. Deadlines that were missed: passive. Deadlines that are being committed to now: active, and in the first person, because that is what a commitment sounds like. The people who get this wrong in either direction are easy to spot. One kind writes a document in which nothing was anybody's fault and nothing is anybody's job. The other writes a document that nobody wants to be quoted in.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: The file was sent to the wrong address, and it was corrected the same afternoon.
The issue was flagged on 3 October, before anybody asked about it.
The deadline was missed. I am accountable for the revised plan.
A temporary workaround has been put in place while we fix the root cause.
The correction was approved by the finance director on Tuesday.
I will circulate the minutes on Friday, with one action item per name.

listenings.text: Here is something nobody teaches you and everybody figures out too late. The minutes are not a record of the meeting. The minutes are the meeting, six months from now, when nobody remembers what was said and somebody is looking for a reason. I have watched a project die because of one sentence in a document that was written in about four seconds by somebody who was not paying attention. It said the delay was caused by the client, with the client's name in it, and it was true, and it was a disaster, because that document went to the client. If it had said the delay was caused by a change in the file format, which was also true and is the same fact, none of it would have happened. Same information. One of them has a person in it and one of them does not.

I write a lot of these and I have one rule that I stole from a lawyer. Anything that went wrong goes in the passive, and anything anybody has to do goes in the active, with a name and a date. The reason is not politeness. It is that a document where nothing is anybody's job is completely useless, and I have read hundreds of those. Everything was reviewed, everything was discussed, everything was agreed, and then nothing happens for three weeks because there is no name anywhere on the page. So: the deadline was missed, that is passive, nobody is on trial. Maria will send the revised plan by Friday, that is active, and now it exists. If I could only keep one of the two rules I would keep the second one, because the first one just avoids a fight and the second one is the only reason anything moves.
